analysis.one_liner: Creates a free, government-run online tax filing and preparation service.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 2022 with 53 cosponsors, all Democrats, the bill was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and never received a markup or vote before Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the IRS to build free online tax filing software, let taxpayers download wage and income data the government already holds, and let people with simple wage-only returns have the IRS prepare and file their return for them. It would also create a short form letting non-filers claim the Earned Income Tax Credit and child tax credit, and bar the IRS from signing any agreement that limits its right to offer these services itself. The bill never got a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who currently pay for commercial tax preparation software or paid preparers, including the large share of filers with simple wage-only returns. Low-income workers and non-filers eligible for the Earned Income Tax Credit or child tax credit would gain a simpler way to claim money they are owed. Taxpayers would also gain access to data the IRS already holds, so they would not have to buy that information back through paid software.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary filers who pay for tax prep

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires the IRS to offer free online tax preparation and filing software, with no fee for any participant, usable year-round and on mobile devices [S3].

It creates a simplified portal that lets people who are not required to file claim the Earned Income Tax Credit and child tax credit without reporting additional income data, with a plain-language, multilingual, mobile-accessible interface [S3].

It lets eligible taxpayers with wage, interest, and dividend income elect to have the IRS prepare their return based on information the government already has, with the taxpayer still submitting and signing off on the final return [S3].

It requires the IRS to make third-party wage and income reports available for download within 15 days of receipt and moves information-return deadlines up to January 31, so taxpayers would have the data they need earlier in filing season [S3].
It prohibits the Treasury Secretary from entering any agreement that restricts the IRS's legal right to provide tax return preparation, software, or filing services [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Commercial tax preparation and filing software companies would lose customers and revenue, starting with the simplest and cheapest returns. Federal taxpayers would fund the IRS software and programs, which the bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' for fiscal years 2022 through 2026 [S3].

drawbacks.text: Building and running the programs is a large, unbudgeted IRS undertaking: the bill authorizes unlimited appropriations through 2026 and sets deadlines as early as March 2023, and the IRS has had well-documented modernization and funding constraints [S3].

The return-prepared-by-IRS program is limited to simple returns: eligible individuals cannot claim deductions for adjusted gross income, must take the standard deduction, cannot file Schedule C, and can have only wages, interest, or dividend income, so self-employed people and itemizers would not qualify at first [S3].

Identity verification is a practical hurdle: the bill requires the IRS to make verification usable by 70 percent of households and 80 percent of EITC-eligible taxpayers within three years, acknowledging that online verification systems have historically excluded some low-income users, and it mandates annual public reporting of pass rates by income and disadvantage group [S3].

Opponents of government-provided filing argue the government writing the tax rules should not also profit from computing the result and that the existing Free File program already covers many filers; the bill addresses this head-on by barring agreements restricting IRS services [S2, S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most filers, the benefit is direct and concrete: free filing, earlier access to their own data, and an easier route to credits they are owed. The main costs are the IRS development budget and the loss of revenue for commercial tax prep companies, plus a real risk that early versions serve only the simplest returns and leave out self-employed and itemizing taxpayers until the programs expand. The design is careful about equity and verification, which addresses but does not eliminate the practical risk of a botched rollout.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Ways and Means Committee for its entire life: it was referred on the day it was introduced, and the committee never reported it out before the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the bill in the House on July 13, 2022 [S5].

The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the same day, and no further action appears in the record: no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
The bill drew 53 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, with no Republican cosponsor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commercial tax preparation and filing software companies are better off because the bill died: the market for paid filing, especially the tens of millions of simple returns, stays with them, and filers continue paying for software or preparers. The IRS also avoids the obligation to build the programs. Nobody else benefits from the outcome.

against.name: Tax preparation and filing software industry

against.what_they_did: Lobbied for years against IRS-provided return-free filing and against allowing the IRS to compete with paid filing products.

sides.party_line_note: All 53 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill's committee of referral took no action.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and filing software companies (Intuit, H&R Block, and similar firms)
industries.note: Free, government-run filing and IRS-prepared returns would take away their core market, starting with the simple, low-cost returns of wage earners. Their interest in keeping paid filing runs against filers' interest in a free alternative, which is why the bill bars agreements restricting IRS services.
Filers would pay nothing for the services but would fund the IRS programs through federal appropriations, which the bill leaves open-ended through 2026.
